[Slide 217] Therac 25
What Went Wrong ?
‑ Race Conditions: A timing bug allowed operators to rapidly change
settings, causing the software to misconfigure the
machine—resulting‑in a high‑dose‑electron beam firing without
proper hardware setup
‑ Integer Overflow / Flag Bug: A control variable tracking hardware
readiness overflowed (from 255 back to 0), tricking the system
into thinking it was safe to deliver radiation even when critical
components weren’t‑in place. Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A
‑ Removal of Hardware Interlocks: Unlike its predecessors
(Therac‑6/20),‑the Therac‑25‑relied solely on software for safety,
eliminating physical safeguards—making‑software bugs lethal
‑ Operator Overconfidence: Cryptic error messages like
“Malfunction‑54”‑appeared frequently but could be bypassed,
leading operators to ignore warnings
‑ Inadequate Testing & Oversight: Safety checks focused on
hardware; software and user interaction were insufficiently tested.
Risk assessments underestimated bug risks by several orders of
magnitude

bundles.window_text:
[Slide 169] Techniques that enable design
‑ Abstraction : Focus on essential properties
‑ Modularity, Cohesion and Coupling
Modularity is the degree or the extent to which the larger module can be decomposed
Cohesion is the glue that keeps the components together. Cohesion which is the extent
to which the component/modules Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A are dependent on/fit into or are related to each
other, when trying to address a specific responsibility (Strong cohesion is good)
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt‑‑‑ooofff‑‑‑CCCSSSEEE‑‑‑–––‑‑‑UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA

[Slide 170] Techniques that enable design
‑ There are seven levels of cohesion of increasing strength:
Coincidental cohesion : With coincidental cohesion, elements are grouped into modules
in a haphazard way. There is no significant relation between the elements.
Logical cohesion : With logical cohesion, the elements realize tasks that are logically
related. One example Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A is a module that contains all input routines. These routines do not
call one another and they do not pass information to each other. Their function is just
very similar.
Temporal cohesion : A typical example of this type of cohesion is an initialization
module. The various elements of it are independent but they are activated at about the
same point in time.
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt‑‑‑ooofff‑‑‑CCCSSSEEE‑‑‑–––‑‑‑UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA

[Slide 171] Techniques that enable design
Procedural cohesion :A module exhibits procedural cohesion if it consists of a number of elements
that have to be executed in some given order. For instance, a module may have to first read some
datum, then search a table, and finally print a result.
Communicational cohesion :This type of cohesion occurs if the elements of a module operate on
the same (external) data. For instance, a module may read some data from a disk, perform certain
computations on those data, and print the result.
Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A
Sequential cohesion :Sequential cohesion occurs if the module consists of a sequence of elements
where the output of one element serves as input to the next element.
Functional cohesion: In a module exhibiting functional cohesion all elements contribute to one
single function of that module. Such a module often transforms a single input datum into a single
output datum. The well-known mathematical subroutines are a typical example of this. Less trivial
examples are modules like ‘execute‑the next edit command’‑and ‘translate‑the program given’.
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt‑‑‑ooofff‑‑‑CCCSSSEEE‑‑‑–––‑‑‑UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA

[Slide 43] Quality management
What is it?
You know quality when you see it, and yet, it can be an elusive thing to define.
But for computer software, quality is something that we must define, and
that’s what we’ll do now.
Who does it?
Everyone—software Department engineers, of CSE – managers, UE23CS341A all stakeholders—involved in the
software process is responsible for quality.
Why is it important?
You can do it right, or you can do it over again. If a software team stresses
quality in all software engineering activities, it reduces the amount of rework
that it must do. That results in lower costs, and more importantly, improved
time to market.
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt ooofff CCCSSSEEE ––– UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA

[Slide 44] RACI matrix
A RACI chart, also called a RACI matrix, is a type of responsibility assignment
matrix (RAM) in project management. In practice, it’s a simple spreadsheet or table
that lists all stakeholders on a project and their level involvement in each task,
denoted with the letters R, A, C or I.
Once these roles are defined, assignments can be attributed to the roles and work
can begin.
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
R, A, C, I stands for:
Responsible
Accountable
Consulted
Informed
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt ooofff CCCSSSEEE ––– UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA

[Slide 45] RACI matrix (Summary)
Responsible is “The Doer” the individual or Individuals who perform an activity —
responsible for an action, there may be several Rs.
Accountable “The Buck Stops Here” The individual who is ultimately Accountable
has the yes/no and power to veto an activity or decision providing the Sponsor is in
agreement. Only one “A” can be assigned to an activity or task as you can't have 2
people driving the bus.
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
Consulted “In the Loop” The individual or individuals who need to be consulted
prior to a task or action being completed their expert knowledge relating to the task
is considered important. This is a two way communication.
Informed The individual or individuals who need(s) to be informed after a decision
or action is taken. One way communication.

[Slide 44] RACI matrix
A RACI chart, also called a RACI matrix, is a type of responsibility assignment
matrix (RAM) in project management. In practice, it’s a simple spreadsheet or table
that lists all stakeholders on a project and their level involvement in each task,
denoted with the letters R, A, C or I.

can begin.

Responsible is “The Doer” the individual or Individuals who perform an activity —
responsible for an action, there may be several Rs.

has the yes/no and power to veto an activity or decision providing the Sponsor is in
agreement. Only one “A” can be assigned to an activity or task as you can't have 2
people driving the bus.

A critical path in a Gantt chart refers to the phenomenon in which any individual task
causes a delay in the related sequence of tasks, thus pushing back a project’s overall
end date.

or floating tasks that Department must be of completed CSE – UE23CS341A in order to get the project done on time.

[Slide 12] Quality of Projects
The project management triangle visualizes the problem of “triple constraints”—the
need to balance scope, cost, and time in order to maintain a high-quality final
product.
Every project manager who has known the frustration of trying to keep their team
productive with too little time, not enough budget, and an impossibly large scope
has experienced the Department project of management CSE – UE23CS341A triangle in action.
No single variable of the project triangle can be changed without making tradeoffs
with the other two points of the triangle.
It’s the project manager’s job to balance all three elements in order to keep their
project within budget and on deadline while still fulfilling the specifications of the
project’s scope.

[Slide 6] Software Project Management
What is a project?
All projects are a temporary effort to create value through a unique product,
service or result. All projects have a beginning and an end. They have a team,
a budget, a schedule and a set of expectations the team needs to meet.
What is project management?
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
Project management is the use of specific knowledge, skills, tools and
techniques to deliver something of value to people.
What is software project management?
Software project management is an art and science of planning and leading
software projects. It is a sub-discipline of project management in
which software projects are planned, implemented, monitored and controlled.
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt ooofff CCCSSSEEE ––– UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA

[Slide 7] Software Project Management
A software project manager :
Defines the requirements of the project,
Builds the project team,
Lays out a blue print for the whole project including the project scope and
parameters,
Clearly communicates the goals of the project to the team; the targets to be
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
achieved,
Allots budget to the various tasks to be completed, and
Ensures that the expectations of the Board of Directors and Stakeholders are
met through timely completion of the project.
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt ooofff CCCSSSEEE ––– UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA

[Slide 8] Software Project Manager – Different roles
Leader
A software project manager must lead his/her team towards success.
He/She should provide them direction and make them understand what is expected of them.
Clearly explain the roles of each member of the team.
He/She must build a team comprising of individuals with different skills so that each member
contributes effectively to the best of their abilities.

The project manager is a link between his/her clients, his/her team and his/her own
supervisors.
He/She must coordinate and transfer all the relevant information from the clients to his/her
team and report to the upper management.
He/She should work closely with analysts, software designers and other staff members and
communicate the goals of the project.

[Slide 33] Project scheduling
Software project scheduling is an activity that distributes estimated effort across the
planned project duration by allocating the effort to specific software engineering tasks.
It is important to note, however, that the schedule evolves over time.
During early stages of project planning, a macroscopic schedule is developed.
This type of schedule identifies all major process framework activities and the product
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
functions to which they are applied .
As the project gets under way, each entry on the macroscopic schedule is refined into a
detailed schedule.
Here, specific software actions and tasks (required to accomplish an activity) are
identified and scheduled.
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt ooofff CCCSSSEEE ––– UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA

[Slide 34] Project scheduling
Scheduling for software engineering projects can be viewed from two rather different
perspectives.
1.
An end date for release of a computer-based system has already (and irrevocably)
been established. The software organization is constrained to distribute effort
within the prescribed time frame.
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
1.
The second view of software assumes that rough chronological bounds have been
discussed but that the end date is set by the software engineering organization.
Effort is distributed to make best use of resources, and an end date is defined after
careful analysis of the software.
Unfortunately, the first situation is encountered far more frequently than the second.

Release planning involves selecting and refining the stories that

bundles.representative_query: What is the difference between measures and metrics in software project estimation?
bundles.window_text:
[Slide 260] Software quality - Terminology
Attribute: measurable physical or abstract property of an entity
Measure: Quantitative indication of extent, amount, dimension, capacity or size
Eg: Number of errors
Metric: Quantitative measure of degree to which a system possesses a given attribute
Calculation between two measures
Eg: number of errors found per person hours
Why measure?
⮚ Feedback: quantifies some of the attribute to help improve the product
⮚ Diagnostics: helps identify issues towards quality
⮚ Supports evaluating and establishing productivity
⮚ Forecasting: to predict future need and anticipate maintenance
⮚ Supports estimating, budgeting, costing and scheduling

[Slide 261] Characteristics of software measure and metrics
⮚
Quantitative: Metrics should be quantitative and expressible in values
⮚
Understandable: Metric computation should be defined and easily understood
⮚
Applicability: Should be applicable at all stages of software development
⮚
Repeatable: Metrics are consistent and same when measured again
⮚
Economical: Computation of metric should be economical
⮚
Language Independent: Metrics should not depend on programming language

[Slide 262] Characteristics of software measure and metrics
Examples of Measures
⮚
Correctness
Defects/KLoC, Failures/Hours of operation
⮚
Maintainability
Mean time to change, Cost to correct
⮚
Integrity
Fault tolerance, security and threats
⮚
Usability
Training time, skill level, productivity

bundles.representative_query: What are the three types of risks based on their nature and source?
bundles.window_text:
[Slide 37] Risk management
Risk management is concerned with identifying risks and drawing
up plans to minimise their effect on a project.
Software risk management is important because of the inherent
uncertainties in software development.
These uncertainties stem from loosely defined requirements,
requirements changes due to changes in customer needs,
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
difficulties in estimating the time and resources required for
software development, and differences in individual skills.
You have to anticipate risks, understand the impact of these risks
on the project, the product and the business, and take steps to
avoid these risks.
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt ooofff CCCSSSEEE ––– UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA

[Slide 38] Risk classification
There are two dimensions of risk classification
The type of risk (technical, organizational, ..)
what is affected by the risk:
Project risks affect schedule or resources;
Product risks affect the quality or performance of the
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
software being developed;
Business risks affect the organisation developing or

bundles.representative_query: What does RACI stand for in a RACI matrix?
bundles.window_text:
[Slide 43] Quality management
What is it?
You know quality when you see it, and yet, it can be an elusive thing to define.
But for computer software, quality is something that we must define, and
that’s what we’ll do now.
Who does it?
Everyone—software Department engineers, of CSE – managers, UE23CS341A all stakeholders—involved in the
software process is responsible for quality.
Why is it important?
You can do it right, or you can do it over again. If a software team stresses
quality in all software engineering activities, it reduces the amount of rework
that it must do. That results in lower costs, and more importantly, improved
time to market.
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt ooofff CCCSSSEEE ––– UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA

[Slide 44] RACI matrix
A RACI chart, also called a RACI matrix, is a type of responsibility assignment
matrix (RAM) in project management. In practice, it’s a simple spreadsheet or table
that lists all stakeholders on a project and their level involvement in each task,
denoted with the letters R, A, C or I.
Once these roles are defined, assignments can be attributed to the roles and work
can begin.
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
R, A, C, I stands for:
Responsible
Accountable
Consulted
Informed
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt ooofff CCCSSSEEE ––– UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA

[Slide 45] RACI matrix (Summary)
Responsible is “The Doer” the individual or Individuals who perform an activity —
responsible for an action, there may be several Rs.
Accountable “The Buck Stops Here” The individual who is ultimately Accountable
has the yes/no and power to veto an activity or decision providing the Sponsor is in
agreement. Only one “A” can be assigned to an activity or task as you can't have 2
people driving the bus.
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
Consulted “In the Loop” The individual or individuals who need to be consulted
prior to a task or action being completed their expert knowledge relating to the task
is considered important. This is a two way communication.
Informed The individual or individuals who need(s) to be informed after a decision
or action is taken. One way communication.
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt ooofff CCCSSSEEE ––– UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA
source_questions: What does RACI stand for in a RACI matrix?

[Slide 6] Software Project Management
What is a project?
All projects are a temporary effort to create value through a unique product,
service or result. All projects have a beginning and an end. They have a team,

[Slide 44] RACI matrix
A RACI chart, also called a RACI matrix, is a type of responsibility assignment
matrix (RAM) in project management. In practice, it’s a simple spreadsheet or table
that lists all stakeholders on a project and their level involvement in each task,
denoted with the letters R, A, C or I.
Once these roles are defined, assignments can be attributed to the roles and work
can begin.
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
R, A, C, I stands for:
Responsible
Accountable
Consulted
Informed
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt ooofff CCCSSSEEE ––– UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA

[Slide 45] RACI matrix (Summary)
Responsible is “The Doer” the individual or Individuals who perform an activity —
responsible for an action, there may be several Rs.
Accountable “The Buck Stops Here” The individual who is ultimately Accountable
has the yes/no and power to veto an activity or decision providing the Sponsor is in
agreement. Only one “A” can be assigned to an activity or task as you can't have 2
people driving the bus.
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
Consulted “In the Loop” The individual or individuals who need to be consulted
prior to a task or action being completed their expert knowledge relating to the task
is considered important. This is a two way communication.
Informed The individual or individuals who need(s) to be informed after a decision
or action is taken. One way communication.

[Slide 50] Gantt Chart
A Gantt chart, commonly used in project management, is one of the most popular
and useful ways of showing activities (tasks or events) displayed against time. On
the left of the chart is a list of the activities and along the top is a suitable time
scale. Each activity is represented by a bar; the position and length of the bar
reflects the start date, duration and end date of the activity. This allows you to see
at a glance:
What the various activities are
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
When each activity begins and ends
How long each activity is scheduled to last
Where activities overlap with other activities, and by how much
The start and end date of the whole project
To summarize, a Gantt chart shows you what has to be done (the activities) and
when (the schedule).

Most software engineering is a group activity
The development schedule for most non-trivial software projects is

Software replaced most hardware-based safety mechanisms.

[Slide 99] Architectural Patterns
What is an Architectural pattern?
An⮚architectural pattern⮚is⮚a⮚general, reusable solution to a commonly occurring
problem in⮚software⮚architecture⮚within⮚a given context.
Following traditional building architecture, a 'software⮚architectural⮚style' is a
specific method of construction, characterized by the features that make it notable.
An architectural style defines: a family of systems in terms of a pattern of structural
organization; a vocabulary of components and connectors, with constraints on how
they can be combined.

[Slide 100] Architectural Patterns
An architectural style is a named collection of architectural design decisions
that are applicable in a given development context,
constrain architectural design decisions that are specific to a particular system
within that context, and
elicit beneficial qualities in each resulting system.
Some treat architectural Department⮚of⮚CSE⮚–⮚UE23CS341A patterns and architectural styles as the same,⮚some⮚treat
styles as specializations of patterns. What they have in common is both patterns and
styles are idioms for architects to use, they "provide a common language"⮚or
"vocabulary"⮚with⮚which to describe classes of systems.
The main difference is that a pattern can be seen as a solution to a problem, while a
style is more general and does not require a problem to solve for its appearance.

[Slide 101] Pipes and Filters Architecture
⮚ Data flows through a sequence
of processing components
(filters), connected by pipes.
⮚ Each filter transforms the input
data and passes it to the next.
⮚ Pipes must compute local
transformations
⮚ Filters must not share state with
other filters
⮚ There must be no cycles

[Slide 99] Architectural Patterns
What is an Architectural pattern?
An⮚architectural pattern⮚is⮚a⮚general, reusable solution to a commonly occurring
problem in⮚software⮚architecture⮚within⮚a given context.
Following traditional building architecture, a 'software⮚architectural⮚style' is a
specific method of construction, characterized by the features that make it notable.
An architectural style defines: a family of systems in terms of a pattern of structural
organization; a vocabulary of components and connectors, with constraints on how
they can be combined.

[Slide 100] Architectural Patterns
An architectural style is a named collection of architectural design decisions
that are applicable in a given development context,
constrain architectural design decisions that are specific to a particular system
within that context, and
elicit beneficial qualities in each resulting system.
Some treat architectural Department⮚of⮚CSE⮚–⮚UE23CS341A patterns and architectural styles as the same,⮚some⮚treat
styles as specializations of patterns. What they have in common is both patterns and
styles are idioms for architects to use, they "provide a common language"⮚or
"vocabulary"⮚with⮚which to describe classes of systems.
The main difference is that a pattern can be seen as a solution to a problem, while a
style is more general and does not require a problem to solve for its appearance.

bundles.representative_query: What are the seven levels of cohesion from weakest to strongest?
bundles.window_text:
[Slide 169] Techniques that enable design
‑ Abstraction : Focus on essential properties
‑ Modularity, Cohesion and Coupling
Modularity is the degree or the extent to which the larger module can be decomposed
Cohesion is the glue that keeps the components together. Cohesion which is the extent
to which the component/modules Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A are dependent on/fit into or are related to each
other, when trying to address a specific responsibility (Strong cohesion is good)
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt‑‑‑ooofff‑‑‑CCCSSSEEE‑‑‑–––‑‑‑UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA

[Slide 170] Techniques that enable design
‑ There are seven levels of cohesion of increasing strength:
Coincidental cohesion : With coincidental cohesion, elements are grouped into modules
in a haphazard way. There is no significant relation between the elements.
Logical cohesion : With logical cohesion, the elements realize tasks that are logically
related. One example Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A is a module that contains all input routines. These routines do not
call one another and they do not pass information to each other. Their function is just
very similar.
Temporal cohesion : A typical example of this type of cohesion is an initialization
module. The various elements of it are independent but they are activated at about the
same point in time.
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt‑‑‑ooofff‑‑‑CCCSSSEEE‑‑‑–––‑‑‑UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA

[Slide 171] Techniques that enable design
Procedural cohesion :A module exhibits procedural cohesion if it consists of a number of elements
that have to be executed in some given order. For instance, a module may have to first read some
datum, then search a table, and finally print a result.
Communicational cohesion :This type of cohesion occurs if the elements of a module operate on
the same (external) data. For instance, a module may read some data from a disk, perform certain
computations on those data, and print the result.
Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A
Sequential cohesion :Sequential cohesion occurs if the module consists of a sequence of elements
where the output of one element serves as input to the next element.
Functional cohesion: In a module exhibiting functional cohesion all elements contribute to one
single function of that module. Such a module often transforms a single input datum into a single
output datum. The well-known mathematical subroutines are a typical example of this. Less trivial
examples are modules like ‘execute‑the next edit command’‑and ‘translate‑the program given’.
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt‑‑‑ooofff‑‑‑CCCSSSEEE‑‑‑–––‑‑‑UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA

[Slide 172] Coupling
‑ Coupling indicates how strongly the modules are connected to other modules. (Loose coupling is
good)
‑ The following types of coupling can be identified (from tightest to loosest):
Content coupling : With content coupling, one module directly affects the working of another
module. Content coupling occurs when a module changes another module’s‑data or when control
is passed from one module Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A to the middle of another (as in a jump). This type of coupling can, and
should, always be avoided.
Common coupling : With common coupling, two modules have shared data. The name originates
from the use of COMMON blocks in FORTRAN. Its equivalent in block-structured languages is the
use of global variables.
External coupling :With external coupling, modules communicate through an external medium,
such as a file.

[Slide 146] Are Microservices always the right choice ?
DDIeeSppFCaarrRtt mmExeeennctt ⮚uootffiv ⮚CCeSSEE ⮚-–⮚UE23CS341A
UEEd2u3cCaSti3o4n1A

[Slide 147] Challenges with a Microservices Architecture
⮚ Increased Operational Complexity - Managing and deploying multiple services
Example:
In a fintech platform, managing independent microservices for payments, authentication, user management,
and analytics requires maintaining separate deployment pipelines and health checks. Any misconfiguration in
one service (e.g., wrong environment variable) could cause cascading failures during deployment
⮚ Inter-Service Communication –⮚Ensuring⮚reliable⮚communication⮚between⮚services
Example:
A microservice for order processing calls an inventory service to check stock. If the inventory service is slow or
down, the order service times out. To mitigate this, developers implement retries with exponential backoff, but
improper configuration can cause a "retry storm," worsening the load on the already degraded service.
⮚ Data Consistency and Integrity - Managing transactions across distributed services
Example:
In an e-commerce platform, placing an order involves updating the order service, inventory, and payment
services. Using a Saga pattern, each service commits locally and compensating transactions are used to roll
back if something fails. If the payment service fails after inventory is deducted, the inventory must be rolled
back separately.

[Slide 148] Challenges with a Microservices Architecture
⮚ Testing and Debugging - End-to-end testing is hard when services depend on each other
Example:
Testing a customer onboarding workflow requires running services like KYC validation, email notification, user
provisioning, and analytics. Mocking each service’s⮚responses is non-trivial, and bugs often emerge only in
staging or production due to real service behavior not matching mocks
⮚ Governance and Standardization –⮚Lack⮚of⮚uniform⮚standards⮚across⮚services
Example:
One team uses REST with camelCase JSON keys (userId), while another uses snake_case (user_id). When
integrating services, the inconsistencies cause serialization/deserialization issues, leading to production bugs and
friction during integration.
⮚ DevOps and Infrastructure Overhead - Managing infrastructure for each service
Example:
Each microservice (e.g., notifications, audit logging, billing) requires its own Dockerfile, Helm charts, CI/CD
pipeline, monitoring dashboards, and alert rules. The operations team spends more time on infrastructure
maintenance than on improving product capabilities

⮚ What is a Component? A component is a replaceable and executable

Replaceable: Can be swapped with other components that provide the
same interface

Black Box: External behavior is defined by interfaces, internal
implementation is hidden
Executable: Participates in system execution

be displayed at the upper right corner.

[Slide 153] Component Interfaces and Interaction Point
⮚ Provided Interfaces: These indicate the functionality a component offers to
other components, shown with a "lollipop" notation.
⮚ Required Interfaces: These indicate the functionality a component needs from
other components to operate correctly, shown with a "socket" notation.
⮚ Connecting Interfaces: Provided and required interfaces can be connected
using an assembly connector. Department⮚of⮚CSE⮚–⮚UE23CS341A
⮚ Ports: A port is an interaction point between a classifier and an external
environment. It groups a semantically cohesive set of provided and required
interfaces.
⮚ Port Notation: A port is denoted as a small square on the boundary of a
classifier. When drawn over the boundary, it indicates public visibility, meaning
all interfaces used are public. If drawn inside, it is either protected or private

bundles.representative_query: What is an API and why is it important in software systems?
bundles.window_text:
[Slide 184] Why Do API and ABI Matter?
‑
System Integration:‑APIs‑and ABIs define how different components of a
software system communicate and interact. APIs govern source-level
interaction, while ABIs handle binary-level interoperability between compiled
modules or external libraries.
‑
Modular Architecture:‑They‑act as contracts between modules—enabling
independent development, easier debugging, testability, and parallel
development workflows. For example, a UI module can call an API of a
business logic module Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A without needing to understand its internals.
‑
Cross-Platform and Cross-Language Interfacing:‑ABI‑compliance ensures that
compiled code (e.g., shared libraries) works across different tools and
platforms. This is vital in environments like Linux, where applications
dynamically link to system libraries.
‑
Example:‑A‑database client written in Python may use a C-based driver library
(via ABI), while exposing a higher-level API to application logic. This layered
separation maintains abstraction and compatibility across updates.
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt‑‑‑ooofff‑‑‑CCCSSSEEE‑‑‑–––‑‑‑UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA 23

[Slide 185] What Is an API?
‑
Definition: An API (Application Programming Interface) is a formal
contract that specifies how different software components
interact. It defines available functions, expected inputs, returned
outputs, error codes, and communication protocols. By
abstracting implementation details, APIs allow modules to evolve
Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A
independently.
‑
Role: APIs act as the boundary between modules, hiding
complexity and presenting a simple interface. This separation
allows teams to work in parallel: one team implements
functionality behind the API, while another consumes it without
knowing internal logic.
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt‑‑‑ooofff‑‑‑CCCSSSEEE‑‑‑–––‑‑‑UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA 24

[Slide 186] Why API Definition Matters
‑ Modularity & Encapsulation: Well-defined APIs enforce encapsulation
by limiting access to only necessary behavior. This minimizes
unintended dependencies and makes the codebase more robust against
changes.
‑ Reusability & Collaboration: Clear API contracts enable reuse of libraries
and components Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A across projects. When teams share an API spec, they
can develop client and server code independently, accelerating delivery
timelines.
‑ Maintainability: Confined behind stable interfaces, internal
implementations can change without impacting consumers. Good
versioning practices further ensure that breaking changes are managed
gracefully.
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt‑‑‑ooofff‑‑‑CCCSSSEEE‑‑‑–––‑‑‑UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA 25

‑ Modularity & Encapsulation: Well-defined APIs enforce encapsulation

changes.
‑ Reusability & Collaboration: Clear API contracts enable reuse of libraries

can develop client and server code independently, accelerating delivery
timelines.
‑ Maintainability: Confined behind stable interfaces, internal
implementations can change without impacting consumers. Good
versioning practices further ensure that breaking changes are managed

DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt‑‑‑ooofff‑‑‑CCCSSSEEE‑‑‑–––‑‑‑UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA 25

[Slide 187] Key Aspects of API Design
‑
Clarity: Use descriptive names and consistent parameter ordering. For
example, choose createUserProfile() over ambiguous names like
userOp(). Clear naming reduces integration errors and enhances
readability.
‑
Simplicity: Expose only essential functions; avoid bloating the interface.
A minimal surface area means fewer integration points to test and
maintain. Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A
‑
Error Handling: Standardize error codes and messages so clients can
programmatically respond to failures. For instance, returning structured
JSON with errorCode and message fields helps clients detect and
handle issues uniformly.
‑
Versioning Strategy: Embed version numbers in API paths or use
semantic versioning in headers. For example, /v1/users vs /v2/users lets
clients opt into new behavior without breaking existing integrations.
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt‑‑‑ooofff‑‑‑CCCSSSEEE‑‑‑–––‑‑‑UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA 26

[Slide 188] Achieving Modularity through API Design
‑
Loose Coupling: Depend only on abstract interfaces rather than
concrete implementations. This allows swapping modules without
rewriting dependent code.
‑
High Cohesion: Group related functionality in the same module and
expose it via cohesive API calls. For example, a UserService API may
offer create, read, update, and delete operations, rather than mixing
unrelated operations. Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A
‑
Information Hiding: Prevent consumers from relying on internal data
structures by providing only accessor methods. This reduces the risk of
breaking clients when internals change.
‑
Extensibility: Use plugin or dependency injection patterns where the
main application consumes modules implementing a common API,
enabling dynamic loading of features.
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt‑‑‑ooofff‑‑‑CCCSSSEEE‑‑‑–––‑‑‑UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA 27

[Slide 295] TDD process activities
⮚
Start by identifying the increment of functionality that is required. This should
normally be small and implementable in a few lines of code.
⮚
Write a test for this functionality and implement this as an automated test.
⮚
Run the test, along with all other tests that have been implemented. Initially,
you have not implemented the functionality so the new test will fail.
⮚
Implement the functionality and re-run the test.
⮚
Once all tests run successfully, you move on to implementing the next chunk
of functionality.

[Slide 296] Benefits of test-driven development
⮚
Code coverage
Every code segment that you write has at least one associated test so all
code written has at least one test.
⮚
Regression testing
A regression test suite is developed incrementally as a program is
developed.
⮚
Simplified debugging
When a test fails, it should be obvious where the problem lies. The newly
written code needs to be checked and modified.
⮚
System documentation
The tests themselves are a form of documentation that describe what the
code should be doing.

[Slide 297] Software Engineering

[Slide 195] Versioning & Compatibility
‑
Backward Compatibility: Newer API versions should accept
requests from older clients without breaking existing
functionality. Techniques include adding optional fields and
keeping default behaviors unchanged.
‑
Forward Compatibility: Older API versions should ignore unknown
Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A
fields sent by newer clients. Protocol buffers handle this
gracefully by skipping unknown tags.
‑
Semantic Versioning: Use MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: increment
MAJOR for incompatible changes, MINOR for backwards-
compatible additions, and PATCH for bug fixes.
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt‑‑‑ooofff‑‑‑CCCSSSEEE‑‑‑–––‑‑‑UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA 34

[Slide 196] Introducing ABI (Application Binary Interface)
‑
Definition & Importance:‑An‑ABI defines low-level details—calling
conventions, data type sizes, symbol names—so‑that
independently compiled binaries can interoperate. Unlike APIs,
ABIs cannot change without breaking binary compatibility.
‑
Impact:‑Changing‑the layout of a struct or the signature of a
Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A
function in a library without updating its ABI can cause crashes or
undefined behaviour in client applications.
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt‑‑‑ooofff‑‑‑CCCSSSEEE‑‑‑–––‑‑‑UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA 35

[Slide 197] Real-World ABI Breakage Examples
‑
OpenSSL 1.1.0 Update (2016):‑Changed‑internal data structures
and removed symbols, breaking compatibility with applications
linking to older versions. Many downstream projects had to
recompile or patch code to restore compatibility.
‑
Glibc SONAME Bump:‑When‑the GNU C Library increments its
SONAME (e.g.,‑libc.so.6‑to‑libc.so.7),‑binaries linked against the
Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A
old SONAME no longer find the library at runtime, causing
widespread failures until re-linked.
‑
LLVM and Clang Tooling:‑Changes‑in symbol visibility and data
layout between minor releases have led some plugins and tools to
break unexpectedly, requiring careful ABI management in plugins.

[Slide 202] Defining Errors in API Contracts
‑
Error Codes & Enums:‑Use‑enumerated types or constants to
define error cases centrally. This ensures consistency across
modules and simplifies both implementation and client-side
handling.
‑
Structured Responses:‑For‑network or IPC APIs, return structured
Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A
payloads (e.g., JSON with‑code,‑message,‑details‑fields)‑so callers
can parse and react programmatically.
‑
Documentation:‑Document‑each error code with its meaning,
range of use, and recovery suggestions to guide developers and
maintain a clear contract.
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt‑‑‑ooofff‑‑‑CCCSSSEEE‑‑‑–––‑‑‑UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA 41

[Slide 203] Error Propagation & Handling Patterns
‑
Return Code Checks:‑In‑procedural languages, functions return
status codes that callers must check. Use helper macros or inline
functions to reduce boilerplate and enforce checks.
‑
Exception-Based Flow:‑In‑OO languages, throw exceptions for
unrecoverable errors, catching them at well-defined boundaries.
This separates normal logic from error-handling code.
Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A
‑
Result/Option Types:‑Functional‑languages or modern languages
(Rust, Swift) use‑Result<T,‑E>‑or‑Option<T>‑to‑encapsulate
success or error, forcing callers to handle both cases explicitly.
‑
HTTP Status Codes:‑REST‑APIs leverage HTTP status codes
(200,‑400,‑500)‑alongside JSON error bodies to indicate success
or failure semantically.
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt‑‑‑ooofff‑‑‑CCCSSSEEE‑‑‑–––‑‑‑UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA 42

[Slide 204] Logging & Observability

Structured Logging:‑Emit‑logs in JSON or key-value pairs,
including fields like‑timestamp,‑error_code,‑module,
and‑stack_trace.‑This supports centralized parsing and alerting.
‑
Error Levels:‑Use‑severity levels (INFO,‑WARN,‑ERROR,‑FATAL)‑to
distinguish recoverable vs. critical failures. Tailor alerts to critical
Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A
levels.
‑
Correlation IDs:‑Attach‑unique request or transaction IDs to log
entries, enabling end-to-end tracing of errors across distributed
or multi-threaded flows.

[Slide 76] System⮚Overview⮚–⮚What⮚is⮚Therac-25?
⮚ Therac-25: Computer-controlled radiation therapy machine.
⮚ Purpose:⮚Deliver⮚controlled⮚dose’s⮚of⮚radiation⮚to⮚cancer⮚patients.
⮚ Design Features:
Software replaced most hardware-based safety mechanisms.
Multiple treatment modes (low-energy X-ray, high-energy electron beam).
Operator used a terminal to input treatment settings.
⮚ Legacy Reuse: Code adapted from Therac-6 and Therac-20, which had physical
safety interlocks.
⮚ Embedded System: Real-time interaction between software and custom
hardware.
⮚ Why this case?
Embedded system with life-critical consequences.
Real-world failures due to poor software architecture.
Lessons applicable to medical, automotive, IoT, and industrial systems.
⮚ Era:⮚1980s,⮚but⮚still⮚cited⮚in⮚safety⮚and⮚architecture⮚literature.

[Slide 77] What Happened?
⮚
Machine delivered massive overdoses of radiation.
⮚
At least 6 incidents, multiple injuries and deaths.
⮚
Software reused from older models, but hardware interlocks
removed.
⮚
System failed silently or with cryptic error messages.

⮚
Tight Coupling:⮚UI,⮚control logic, and machine control shared
global memory.
⮚
Race Conditions:⮚Unsafe⮚state transitions when operators acted
quickly.
⮚
Reused Legacy Code:⮚Assumed⮚hardware interlocks would catch
errors.
⮚
Lack of Fault Isolation:⮚No⮚module⮚validation⮚or⮚error⮚containment.
⮚
Poor Observability:⮚No⮚logging⮚or⮚diagnostics.

bundles.representative_query: What are the six process activities in TDD?
bundles.window_text:
[Slide 294] Test-driven Development

[Slide 295] TDD process activities
⮚
Start by identifying the increment of functionality that is required. This should
normally be small and implementable in a few lines of code.
⮚
Write a test for this functionality and implement this as an automated test.
⮚
Run the test, along with all other tests that have been implemented. Initially,
you have not implemented the functionality so the new test will fail.
⮚
Implement the functionality and re-run the test.
⮚
Once all tests run successfully, you move on to implementing the next chunk
of functionality.

[Slide 296] Benefits of test-driven development
⮚
Code coverage
Every code segment that you write has at least one associated test so all
code written has at least one test.
⮚
Regression testing
A regression test suite is developed incrementally as a program is
developed.
⮚
Simplified debugging
When a test fails, it should be obvious where the problem lies. The newly
written code needs to be checked and modified.
⮚
System documentation
The tests themselves are a form of documentation that describe what the
code should be doing.

bundles.representative_query: What are the four benefits of Test-Driven Development?
bundles.window_text:
[Slide 293] Test-driven Development
⮚
Test-driven development (TDD) is an approach to program development in
which you inter-leave testing and code development.
⮚
Tests are written before code and ‘passing’⮚the tests is the critical driver of
development.
⮚
You develop code incrementally, along with a test for that increment. You
don’t⮚move on to the next increment until the code that you have developed
passes its test.
⮚
TDD was introduced as part of agile methods such as Extreme Programming.
However, it can also be used in plan-driven development processes.

[Slide 33] Project scheduling
Software project scheduling is an activity that distributes estimated effort across the
planned project duration by allocating the effort to specific software engineering tasks.
It is important to note, however, that the schedule evolves over time.
During early stages of project planning, a macroscopic schedule is developed.
This type of schedule identifies all major process framework activities and the product
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
functions to which they are applied .
As the project gets under way, each entry on the macroscopic schedule is refined into a
detailed schedule.
Here, specific software actions and tasks (required to accomplish an activity) are
identified and scheduled.
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt ooofff CCCSSSEEE ––– UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA

[Slide 34] Project scheduling
Scheduling for software engineering projects can be viewed from two rather different
perspectives.
1.
An end date for release of a computer-based system has already (and irrevocably)
been established. The software organization is constrained to distribute effort
within the prescribed time frame.
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
1.
The second view of software assumes that rough chronological bounds have been
discussed but that the end date is set by the software engineering organization.
Effort is distributed to make best use of resources, and an end date is defined after
careful analysis of the software.
Unfortunately, the first situation is encountered far more frequently than the second.
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt ooofff CCCSSSEEE ––– UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA

[Slide 22] Task allocation
During the task planning stage, the developers break down
stories into development tasks.
A development task should take 4–16 hours.
All of the tasks that must be completed to implement all of the
stories in that iteration are listed.

The individual developers then sign up for the specific tasks that
they will implement.
Benefits of this approach:
The whole team gets an overview of the tasks to be completed in
an iteration.
Developers have a sense of ownership in these tasks and this is
likely to motivate them to complete the task.

A software increment is always delivered at the end of each

bundles.representative_query: Explain the three steps of TDD development cycle.
bundles.window_text:
[Slide 294] Test-driven Development

[Slide 295] TDD process activities
⮚
Start by identifying the increment of functionality that is required. This should
normally be small and implementable in a few lines of code.
⮚
Write a test for this functionality and implement this as an automated test.
⮚
Run the test, along with all other tests that have been implemented. Initially,
you have not implemented the functionality so the new test will fail.
⮚
Implement the functionality and re-run the test.
⮚
Once all tests run successfully, you move on to implementing the next chunk
of functionality.

[Slide 296] Benefits of test-driven development
⮚
Code coverage
Every code segment that you write has at least one associated test so all
code written has at least one test.
⮚
Regression testing
A regression test suite is developed incrementally as a program is
developed.
⮚
Simplified debugging
When a test fails, it should be obvious where the problem lies. The newly
written code needs to be checked and modified.
⮚
System documentation
The tests themselves are a form of documentation that describe what the
code should be doing.

bundles.representative_query: How does TDD prevent regression bugs from being introduced?
bundles.window_text:
[Slide 295] TDD process activities
⮚
Start by identifying the increment of functionality that is required. This should
normally be small and implementable in a few lines of code.
⮚
Write a test for this functionality and implement this as an automated test.
⮚
Run the test, along with all other tests that have been implemented. Initially,
you have not implemented the functionality so the new test will fail.
⮚
Implement the functionality and re-run the test.
⮚
Once all tests run successfully, you move on to implementing the next chunk
of functionality.

[Slide 296] Benefits of test-driven development
⮚
Code coverage
Every code segment that you write has at least one associated test so all
code written has at least one test.
⮚
Regression testing
A regression test suite is developed incrementally as a program is
developed.
⮚
Simplified debugging
When a test fails, it should be obvious where the problem lies. The newly
written code needs to be checked and modified.
⮚
System documentation
The tests themselves are a form of documentation that describe what the
code should be doing.

A RACI chart, also called a RACI matrix, is a type of responsibility assignment
matrix (RAM) in project management. In practice, it’s a simple spreadsheet or table
that lists all stakeholders on a project and their level involvement in each task,
denoted with the letters R, A, C or I.
Once these roles are defined, assignments can be attributed to the roles and work
can begin.
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
R, A, C, I stands for:
Responsible
Accountable
Consulted
Informed

[Slide 45] RACI matrix (Summary)
Responsible is “The Doer” the individual or Individuals who perform an activity —
responsible for an action, there may be several Rs.
Accountable “The Buck Stops Here” The individual who is ultimately Accountable
has the yes/no and power to veto an activity or decision providing the Sponsor is in
agreement. Only one “A” can be assigned to an activity or task as you can't have 2
people driving the bus.
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
Consulted “In the Loop” The individual or individuals who need to be consulted
prior to a task or action being completed their expert knowledge relating to the task
is considered important. This is a two way communication.
Informed The individual or individuals who need(s) to be informed after a decision
or action is taken. One way communication.

[Slide 7] Software Project Management
A software project manager :
Defines the requirements of the project,
Builds the project team,
Lays out a blue print for the whole project including the project scope and
parameters,
Clearly communicates the goals of the project to the team; the targets to be
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
achieved,
Allots budget to the various tasks to be completed, and
Ensures that the expectations of the Board of Directors and Stakeholders are

[Slide 8] Software Project Manager – Different roles
Leader
A software project manager must lead his/her team towards success.
He/She should provide them direction and make them understand what is expected of them.
Clearly explain the roles of each member of the team.
He/She must build a team comprising of individuals with different skills so that each member
contributes effectively to the best of their abilities.
Liaison Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
The project manager is a link between his/her clients, his/her team and his/her own
supervisors.
He/She must coordinate and transfer all the relevant information from the clients to his/her
team and report to the upper management.
He/She should work closely with analysts, software designers and other staff members and
communicate the goals of the project.
He/She monitors the progress of the project, taking action accordingly.

Mentor
He/She must be there to guide his/her team at every step and ensure that the team has
cohesion.
He/She provides advice to his/her team wherever they need it and points them in the
right direction.

[Slide 17] Agile Planning
Release planning, which looks ahead for several months and
decides on the features that should be included in a release of a
system.
Iteration planning, which has a shorter-term outlook, and focuses
on planning the next increment of a system. This is typically 2-4
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
weeks of work for the team.

[Slide 18] Approaches to Agile Planning
Planning in Scrum
Based on managing a project backlog (things to be done) with
daily reviews of progress and problems
The planning game
Developed originally as part of Extreme Programming (XP)
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
Dependent on user stories as a measure of progress in the project
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt ooofff CCCSSSEEE ––– UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA

[Slide 19] Story based Planning
The planning game is based on user stories that reflect the
features that should be included in the system.
The project team read and discuss the stories and rank them in
order of the amount of time they think it will take to implement
the story.
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
Stories are assigned ‘effort points’ reflecting their size and
difficulty of implementation
The number of effort points implemented per day is measured
giving an estimate of the team’s ‘velocity’
This allows the total effort required to implement the system to
be estimated

Risk management is concerned with identifying risks and drawing
up plans to minimise their effect on a project.
Software risk management is important because of the inherent
uncertainties in software development.
These uncertainties stem from loosely defined requirements,
requirements changes due to changes in customer needs,
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
difficulties in estimating the time and resources required for
software development, and differences in individual skills.
You have to anticipate risks, understand the impact of these risks
on the project, the product and the business, and take steps to
avoid these risks.

The type of risk (technical, organizational, ..)
what is affected by the risk:
Project risks affect schedule or resources;
Product risks affect the quality or performance of the
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
software being developed;
Business risks affect the organisation developing or
procuring the software.

bundles.representative_query: Why do microservices require independent CI/CD pipelines for each service?
bundles.window_text:
[Slide 147] Challenges with a Microservices Architecture
⮚ Increased Operational Complexity - Managing and deploying multiple services
Example:
In a fintech platform, managing independent microservices for payments, authentication, user management,
and analytics requires maintaining separate deployment pipelines and health checks. Any misconfiguration in
one service (e.g., wrong environment variable) could cause cascading failures during deployment
⮚ Inter-Service Communication –⮚Ensuring⮚reliable⮚communication⮚between⮚services
Example:
A microservice for order processing calls an inventory service to check stock. If the inventory service is slow or
down, the order service times out. To mitigate this, developers implement retries with exponential backoff, but
improper configuration can cause a "retry storm," worsening the load on the already degraded service.
⮚ Data Consistency and Integrity - Managing transactions across distributed services
Example:
In an e-commerce platform, placing an order involves updating the order service, inventory, and payment
services. Using a Saga pattern, each service commits locally and compensating transactions are used to roll
back if something fails. If the payment service fails after inventory is deducted, the inventory must be rolled
back separately.

[Slide 148] Challenges with a Microservices Architecture
⮚ Testing and Debugging - End-to-end testing is hard when services depend on each other
Example:
Testing a customer onboarding workflow requires running services like KYC validation, email notification, user
provisioning, and analytics. Mocking each service’s⮚responses is non-trivial, and bugs often emerge only in
staging or production due to real service behavior not matching mocks
⮚ Governance and Standardization –⮚Lack⮚of⮚uniform⮚standards⮚across⮚services
Example:
One team uses REST with camelCase JSON keys (userId), while another uses snake_case (user_id). When
integrating services, the inconsistencies cause serialization/deserialization issues, leading to production bugs and
friction during integration.
⮚ DevOps and Infrastructure Overhead - Managing infrastructure for each service
Example:
Each microservice (e.g., notifications, audit logging, billing) requires its own Dockerfile, Helm charts, CI/CD
pipeline, monitoring dashboards, and alert rules. The operations team spends more time on infrastructure
maintenance than on improving product capabilities

[Slide 149] Challenges with a Microservices Architecture
Team and Organizational Challenges - Coordination and skill gaps between teams
Example:
A team responsible for the billing microservice decides to upgrade to a new database version. However, they
fail to notify the data ingestion team, whose service depends on specific billing data formats. This causes
downstream failures during deployment
Versioning and Backward Compatibility – Managing breaking changes across services
Example:
A user profile service renames a field from fullName to name. Several consuming services, including
notifications and analytics, break because they were not updated in time. Even with versioned APIs,
maintaining compatibility across consumers is difficult.
Security and Compliance - Securing communication and enforcing compliance across services
Example:
In a healthcare system, services like patient data, prescription management, and reporting must all comply with
HIPAA. If the report-generation service accidentally logs sensitive patient data without encryption or access
control, it can lead to a major compliance violation
source_questions: Why do microservices require independent CI/CD pipelines for each service?

bundles.window_text:
[Slide 169] Techniques that enable design
‑ Abstraction : Focus on essential properties
‑ Modularity, Cohesion and Coupling
Modularity is the degree or the extent to which the larger module can be decomposed
Cohesion is the glue that keeps the components together. Cohesion which is the extent
to which the component/modules Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A are dependent on/fit into or are related to each
other, when trying to address a specific responsibility (Strong cohesion is good)
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt‑‑‑ooofff‑‑‑CCCSSSEEE‑‑‑–––‑‑‑UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA

[Slide 170] Techniques that enable design
‑ There are seven levels of cohesion of increasing strength:
Coincidental cohesion : With coincidental cohesion, elements are grouped into modules
in a haphazard way. There is no significant relation between the elements.
Logical cohesion : With logical cohesion, the elements realize tasks that are logically
related. One example Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A is a module that contains all input routines. These routines do not
call one another and they do not pass information to each other. Their function is just
very similar.
Temporal cohesion : A typical example of this type of cohesion is an initialization
module. The various elements of it are independent but they are activated at about the
same point in time.
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt‑‑‑ooofff‑‑‑CCCSSSEEE‑‑‑–––‑‑‑UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA

[Slide 171] Techniques that enable design
Procedural cohesion :A module exhibits procedural cohesion if it consists of a number of elements
that have to be executed in some given order. For instance, a module may have to first read some
datum, then search a table, and finally print a result.
Communicational cohesion :This type of cohesion occurs if the elements of a module operate on
the same (external) data. For instance, a module may read some data from a disk, perform certain
computations on those data, and print the result.
Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A
Sequential cohesion :Sequential cohesion occurs if the module consists of a sequence of elements
where the output of one element serves as input to the next element.
Functional cohesion: In a module exhibiting functional cohesion all elements contribute to one
single function of that module. Such a module often transforms a single input datum into a single
output datum. The well-known mathematical subroutines are a typical example of this. Less trivial
examples are modules like ‘execute‑the next edit command’‑and ‘translate‑the program given’.
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt‑‑‑ooofff‑‑‑CCCSSSEEE‑‑‑–––‑‑‑UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA

[Slide 172] Coupling
‑ Coupling indicates how strongly the modules are connected to other modules. (Loose coupling is
good)
‑ The following types of coupling can be identified (from tightest to loosest):
Content coupling : With content coupling, one module directly affects the working of another
module. Content coupling occurs when a module changes another module’s‑data or when control
is passed from one module Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A to the middle of another (as in a jump). This type of coupling can, and
should, always be avoided.
Common coupling : With common coupling, two modules have shared data. The name originates
from the use of COMMON blocks in FORTRAN. Its equivalent in block-structured languages is the
use of global variables.
External coupling :With external coupling, modules communicate through an external medium,
such as a file.

[Slide 203] Error Propagation & Handling Patterns
‑
Return Code Checks:‑In‑procedural languages, functions return
status codes that callers must check. Use helper macros or inline
functions to reduce boilerplate and enforce checks.
‑
Exception-Based Flow:‑In‑OO languages, throw exceptions for
unrecoverable errors, catching them at well-defined boundaries.
This separates normal logic from error-handling code.
Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A
‑
Result/Option Types:‑Functional‑languages or modern languages
(Rust, Swift) use‑Result<T,‑E>‑or‑Option<T>‑to‑encapsulate
success or error, forcing callers to handle both cases explicitly.
‑
HTTP Status Codes:‑REST‑APIs leverage HTTP status codes
(200,‑400,‑500)‑alongside JSON error bodies to indicate success
or failure semantically.

‑
Structured Logging:‑Emit‑logs in JSON or key-value pairs,
including fields like‑timestamp,‑error_code,‑module,
and‑stack_trace.‑This supports centralized parsing and alerting.
‑
Error Levels:‑Use‑severity levels (INFO,‑WARN,‑ERROR,‑FATAL)‑to
distinguish recoverable vs. critical failures. Tailor alerts to critical
Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A
levels.

Correlation IDs:‑Attach‑unique request or transaction IDs to log
entries, enabling end-to-end tracing of errors across distributed
or multi-threaded flows.

duplication.

bundles.representative_query: What does the Therac-25 teach about the dangers of insufficient regression testing?
bundles.window_text:
[Slide 295] TDD process activities
⮚
Start by identifying the increment of functionality that is required. This should
normally be small and implementable in a few lines of code.
⮚
Write a test for this functionality and implement this as an automated test.
⮚
Run the test, along with all other tests that have been implemented. Initially,
you have not implemented the functionality so the new test will fail.
⮚
Implement the functionality and re-run the test.
⮚
Once all tests run successfully, you move on to implementing the next chunk
of functionality.

[Slide 296] Benefits of test-driven development
⮚
Code coverage
Every code segment that you write has at least one associated test so all
code written has at least one test.
⮚
Regression testing
A regression test suite is developed incrementally as a program is
developed.
⮚
Simplified debugging
When a test fails, it should be obvious where the problem lies. The newly
written code needs to be checked and modified.
⮚
System documentation
The tests themselves are a form of documentation that describe what the
code should be doing.

[Slide 184] Why Do API and ABI Matter?
‑
System Integration:‑APIs‑and ABIs define how different components of a
software system communicate and interact. APIs govern source-level
interaction, while ABIs handle binary-level interoperability between compiled
modules or external libraries.
‑
Modular Architecture:‑They‑act as contracts between modules—enabling
independent development, easier debugging, testability, and parallel
development workflows. For example, a UI module can call an API of a
business logic module Department‑of‑CSE‑–‑UE23CS341A without needing to understand its internals.
‑
Cross-Platform and Cross-Language Interfacing:‑ABI‑compliance ensures that
compiled code (e.g., shared libraries) works across different tools and
platforms. This is vital in environments like Linux, where applications
dynamically link to system libraries.
‑
Example:‑A‑database client written in Python may use a C-based driver library
(via ABI), while exposing a higher-level API to application logic. This layered
separation maintains abstraction and compatibility across updates.

[Slide 12] Quality of Projects
The project management triangle visualizes the problem of “triple constraints”—the
need to balance scope, cost, and time in order to maintain a high-quality final
product.
Every project manager who has known the frustration of trying to keep their team
productive with too little time, not enough budget, and an impossibly large scope
has experienced the Department project of management CSE – UE23CS341A triangle in action.
No single variable of the project triangle can be changed without making tradeoffs
with the other two points of the triangle.
It’s the project manager’s job to balance all three elements in order to keep their
project within budget and on deadline while still fulfilling the specifications of the
project’s scope.

[Slide 37] Risk management
Risk management is concerned with identifying risks and drawing
up plans to minimise their effect on a project.
Software risk management is important because of the inherent
uncertainties in software development.
These uncertainties stem from loosely defined requirements,
requirements changes due to changes in customer needs,
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
difficulties in estimating the time and resources required for
software development, and differences in individual skills.
You have to anticipate risks, understand the impact of these risks
on the project, the product and the business, and take steps to
avoid these risks.

The type of risk (technical, organizational, ..)
what is affected by the risk:
Project risks affect schedule or resources;
Product risks affect the quality or performance of the

software being developed;
Business risks affect the organisation developing or
procuring the software.

[Slide 33] Project scheduling
Software project scheduling is an activity that distributes estimated effort across the
planned project duration by allocating the effort to specific software engineering tasks.
It is important to note, however, that the schedule evolves over time.
During early stages of project planning, a macroscopic schedule is developed.
This type of schedule identifies all major process framework activities and the product
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
functions to which they are applied .
As the project gets under way, each entry on the macroscopic schedule is refined into a
detailed schedule.
Here, specific software actions and tasks (required to accomplish an activity) are
identified and scheduled.
DDDeeepppaaarrrtttmmmeeennnttt ooofff CCCSSSEEE ––– UUUEEE222333CCCSSS333444111AAA

[Slide 34] Project scheduling
Scheduling for software engineering projects can be viewed from two rather different
perspectives.
1.
An end date for release of a computer-based system has already (and irrevocably)
been established. The software organization is constrained to distribute effort
within the prescribed time frame.
Department of CSE – UE23CS341A
1.
The second view of software assumes that rough chronological bounds have been
discussed but that the end date is set by the software engineering organization.
Effort is distributed to make best use of resources, and an end date is defined after
careful analysis of the software.
Unfortunately, the first situation is encountered far more frequently than the second.
